content: The potato refers to the starchy tuberous crop derived from the perennial plant Solanum tuberosum, which belongs to the Solanaceae family, commonly known as the nightshade family. It is also the name for the plant itself. Potatoes are the most widely cultivated tuber crop globally and rank as the fourth largest food crop in terms of fresh produce, following rice, wheat, and maize. The potato originated in the region of modern-day Peru and spread from South America to Spain, and subsequently to the rest of the world, following European colonization in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. In the Southern Bolivian town of San Andreas, up to 300 potato varieties are displayed annually at the town's potato festival. Over time, the potato became a critical food staple and agricultural crop. For example, it served as a primary food source for sailors aboard Spanish ships. After the Spanish Armada's wreck in 1588, Irish coastal villagers salvaged potatoes and began cultivating them. However, in 1845, the fungal disease Phytophthora infestans, also known as late blight, devastated potato crops in western Ireland, leading to the Great Irish Famine. The local population, heavily reliant on potatoes, suffered catastrophic losses, with many dying and others emigrating, primarily to the United States, often blaming the British government for their plight. Potatoes are also closely associated with regions such as Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Prince Edward Island, Ireland, Jersey, and Russia due to their significant role in the agricultural economies and histories of these areas. The English term potato originates from the Spanish word patata, which itself derives from the Nahuatl word potatl, likely the tuber's original name. In contrast, the Bulgarian картоф, Russian картофель, and German Kartoffel trace their roots to the Italian word tartufoli, named for the potato's resemblance to truffles (tartufo in Italian). Other names for the potato include ground apple, as seen in French (pomme de terre), Dutch (aardappel), Hebrew (תפוח אדמה), and Austrian German (Erdapfel). In Finnish, the term peruna stems from the old Swedish jordpäron, meaning earth pear. In 16th-century French, pomme referred to fruit, and pomme de terre literally meant ground fruit, a term likely translated into other languages as potatoes were introduced. In Polish, the potato is called ziemniaki, and in Slovak, zemiak, both derived from the word for ground. In northern Indian languages and Nepali, the potato is known as alu, while in Indonesian, it is called kentang. In China, the potato has various regional names, with the most common in standard Chinese being horse-bell yam (马铃薯 mǎlíngshǔ), earth bean (土豆 tǔdòu), and foreign taro (洋芋 yángyù). Potato plants grow above ground and produce flowers ranging from yellow to silver, with yellow stamens. Cross-pollination occurs primarily through bumblebees, although self-fertilization is also common. Potatoes can be propagated vegetatively by planting tubers or tuber pieces containing at least one or two eyes, or through cuttings, a method often used in greenhouses to produce healthy seed tubers. Some commercial potato varieties do not produce seeds due to imperfect flowers and are propagated exclusively from tuber pieces, which are referred to as seed potatoes. After flowering, certain potato varieties produce small green fruits resembling green cherry tomatoes, each containing up to 300 true seeds. These seeds can be extracted by blending the fruits with water, allowing the seeds to sink while the fruit pulp floats. New potato varieties are cultivated from these seeds, also known as true seed or botanical seed, to differentiate them from seed tubers. The potato's origin is widely agreed upon by botanists to be the Andes, spanning from Colombia to northern Argentina, with a concentration of genetic diversity in modern-day Peru. Andean potatoes are not all of the same species. The primary species is Solanum tuberosum ssp. andigena (a tetraploid with 48 chromosomes). Additionally, there are four diploid species (Solanum stenotomum, Solanum phureja, Solanum goniocalyx, and Solanum ajanhuiri), two triploid species (Solanum chaucha and Solanum juzepczukii), and one pentaploid species (Solanum curtilobum). Andean potatoes are adapted to short-day conditions, while Chilean potatoes thrive under long-day conditions. Evidence suggests that the tetraploid Andean short-day potato was the first to reach Southern Spain around 1565, from where it spread across Europe, adapting to long-day conditions over approximately 200 years. Taxonomists have classified potatoes into two subspecies: Solanum tuberosum ssp. tuberosum (long-day adapted) and Solanum tuberosum ssp. andigena (short-day adapted). These subspecies differ morphologically, though the distinctions are subtle and require expert observation. Russian taxonomists in the early 20th century even classified them as separate species: Solanum tuberosum and Solanum andigenum. The adaptation to long-day conditions occurred once before, as the potato spread from the Andes to southern South America before European colonization. Chile retains a significant repository of potato germplasm adapted to long days. Historical and genetic evidence indicates that the potato reached India shortly after its introduction to Europe, likely brought by the Portuguese. In isolated Himalayan regions of India and Nepal, desi potatoes, similar to the short-day adapted Andean potato (Solanum tuberosum ssp. andigena), are still cultivated. Globally, there are approximately 5,000 potato varieties, with 3,000 found in the Andes alone, primarily in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and Colombia. These varieties belong to eight or nine species, depending on the taxonomic classification. Additionally, there are about 200 wild potato species, many of which have been crossbred with cultivated species to introduce pest and disease resistance. However, the varieties available in European, North American, and Asian markets are limited and belong to the same species, Solanum tuberosum ssp. tuberosum. These are often referred to as Irish potatoes in English-speaking regions due to their association with the Great Irish Famine. During this famine, the Irish peasant population, heavily reliant on potatoes, suffered devastating losses when the late blight fungus (Phytophthora infestans) destroyed crops. The famine's long-term effects are well-documented, including the role of British landowners who continued exporting grain from Ireland during the crisis. Most modern potatoes in North America were introduced through European settlement rather than directly from South America. Nonetheless, one wild potato species, Solanum fendleri, found as far north as Texas, has been used in breeding programs for nematode resistance. Mexico serves as a secondary center of genetic variability for potatoes, with wild species like the hexaploid Solanum demissum extensively used in breeding for late blight resistance. The potato became a vital staple crop in northern Europe during the Little Ice Age when traditional crops failed to produce reliably. Potatoes often succeeded in providing food during colder years when other crops failed. However, the potato was not widely adopted in France during this period, and some famines might have been mitigated had French farmers embraced the crop. Today, the potato is integral to the traditional cuisines of the British Isles, northern, central, and eastern Europe. As of 2007, Germany had the highest per capita potato consumption globally.
